entries.title: Students in a course
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 2, Table 2.1 and Table 2.2, Fig. 2.2a
entries.teaches: An equivalence relation on a named set, given by Klir as a set, as a matrix, and as a node-edge diagram — the same system in three registers, with the relation partitioning the set into equivalence classes.

entries.title: Goal-oriented systems — the Informationless paradigm
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 10 §10.2, Fig. 10.1
entries.teaches: The most restrictive of Klir's four goal-oriented paradigms: the goal-seeking element emits its variable blind, receiving neither the input nor the output it is trying to influence.

entries.title: Goal-oriented systems — the Feedback paradigm
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 10 §10.2, Fig. 10.1
entries.teaches: The goal-seeking element reads the output variable, so it can react to undesirable changes in the output but has no mechanism for anticipating them.

entries.title: Goal-oriented systems — the Feedforward paradigm
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 10 §10.2, Fig. 10.1
entries.teaches: The goal-seeking element reads the input variable, letting it anticipate the output rather than only react to it.

entries.title: Goal-oriented systems — the Full-information paradigm
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 10 §10.2, Fig. 10.1
entries.teaches: The least restrictive paradigm: the goal-seeking element reads both the input and the output, combining anticipation with reaction.

entries.title: The two-thing system — a acts on b
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §1.2, Definition 1.2, Example, Fig. 1.2
entries.teaches: The simplest possible system in Bunge's words: two connected things in an environment lumped into a single thing, with the internal structure a▷b — a acts on b, and not conversely.

entries.title: The two-thing system — b acts on a
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §1.2, Definition 1.2, Example, Fig. 1.2
entries.teaches: The same composition and environment as its siblings, with the internal structure reversed to b▷a — showing that structure, not composition, is what distinguishes these systems.

entries.title: The two-thing system — a and b act on each other
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §1.2, Definition 1.2, Example, Fig. 1.2
entries.teaches: The same composition and environment again, with the reciprocal internal structure a⋈b — the third and last of the conceivable internal structures on two things.

entries.title: Coupling graph σ₁ — a symmetric chain
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §2.1, Coupling Graphs and Matrices
entries.teaches: The first of Bunge's three coupling examples: a system given as a graph and, equivalently, as a matrix. Every coupling is mutual and excitatory, so the matrix is symmetric and the graph is an undirected chain.

entries.title: Coupling graph σ₂ — a cycle with inhibition
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §2.1, Coupling Graphs and Matrices
entries.teaches: Bunge's second coupling example: four components in a directed cycle where two of the four couplings are inhibitory rather than excitatory, entered in the matrix as −1 against +1.

entries.title: Coupling graph σ₃ — self-action and feedback
entries.citation: Mario Bunge, Treatise on Basic Philosophy, Vol. 4: A World of Systems (1979), Ch. 1 §2.1, Coupling Graphs and Matrices
entries.teaches: Bunge's third coupling example, and the one that reads differently in two traditions: components 2 and 3 each act on themselves, and act on each other. His caption — "the loops indicate self action or feedback" — names both at once, and both are legal Bunge structure.

entries.title: A cell in a cellular array
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 4, book pp. 83–84, Fig. 4.11
entries.teaches: That the environment is placed by the observer, not found in the world. This cell's environment is four OTHER CELLS OF THE SAME ARRAY — nothing distinguishes inside from outside except where the investigator drew the boundary, and the same 5×5 array admits 2²⁵ different structure systems depending on which subset of cells is chosen.

entries.title: A serial binary adder
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 4, book pp. 78–79, Fig. 4.8
entries.teaches: A cycle as pure structure. The carry leaves CARRY, is held one discrete time by MEMORY, and returns as the previous carry that both SUM and CARRY depend on — a loop that exists in the wiring, with no dynamics run and no state stored anywhere in this model.

entries.title: Criminal courts and probation, New York State
entries.citation: George Klir, Facets of Systems Science, 2nd ed. (2001), Ch. 4, book pp. 77–78, Fig. 4.7
entries.teaches: A structure system in Klir's own sense: five elements, ten directed variables, and a feedback edge, over an institutional domain rather than a physical one. Each variable is an output of exactly one element — Klir's own legality rule for structure systems, checkable against this model.

entries.title: The Steel-Plant in its environment
entries.citation: George Mobus, Systems Science: Theory, Analysis, Modeling, and Design (2022), Ch. 4 §4.5, Fig. 4.14 and Listing 4.1
entries.teaches: Mobus's own worked exemplar for SL, at the level the figure draws it: the SOI Steel-Plant as an opaque box situated among three environmental sources and three sinks, with electric energy, iron and coke crossing in and steel, scrap and waste heat crossing out. Six flows, six environment entities, one boundary — the whole of level -1, and nothing beneath it.

entries.title: A digital computing system
entries.citation: George Mobus, Systems Science: Theory, Analysis, Modeling, and Design (2022), Ch. 7 §7.2.3–§7.2.3.1, Figs. 7.2 and 7.3
entries.teaches: The first rung of the chapter's ladder — a MERELY COMPLEX system, analysed only as far as level 1. What the reader should notice is how little the first pass contains and how much it already fixes: the boundary, the four environmental entities Mobus names (wall socket, file device, users, heat), the direction of every crossing flow, and the three internal components (hardware, software, and the firmware that couples them). Nothing here adapts or evolves; that is the point of starting here.

entries.title: A "typical" neuron
entries.citation: George Mobus, Systems Science: Theory, Analysis, Modeling, and Design (2022), Ch. 7 §7.3.2–§7.3.3.1, Figs. 7.7 and 7.8
entries.teaches: The second rung — a COMPLEX ADAPTIVE system at the same level 1 as the computer, and the diff against it is the lesson. The composition is no larger, but the environment is now made of things of the SAME KIND as the SOI (other neurons are its sources and sinks), and one flow runs backwards: the membrane feeds its temporal correlation back to the synapses, which is where adaptation lives. A synapse's response strength "depends on the history of activations at each one" — history, in a structural model, shows up only as that returning edge.

entries.title: The mammalian brain — the afferent visual path
entries.citation: George Mobus, Systems Science: Theory, Analysis, Modeling, and Design (2022), Ch. 7 §7.4.4–§7.4.5, Figs. 7.12 and 7.13
entries.teaches: The third rung — a COMPLEX ADAPTIVE AND EVOLVABLE system, and the one entry in this set that does not close. Mobus walks a single message path into the brain and stops; the model stops with him, and the last cortical stage is left hanging. What the reader should notice is that the boundary is the hard part here, not the components: the brain is "a system that has a seemingly clear physical boundary but in fact is so highly porous and fuzzy that identification of real boundaries is a major challenge" (§7.1), and it is footnote 8, not any figure, that finally fixes it — brain proper is the SOI, the rest of the CNS and all of the PNS are sources and sinks.

entries.title: The human social system in the Ecos
entries.citation: George Mobus, Systems Science: Theory, Analysis, Modeling, and Design (2022), Ch. 7 §7.6.3, Fig. 7.17
entries.teaches: The last rung — the whole human enterprise as one SOI inside the Earth, and the only entry in the set whose lesson is an ABSENCE. Resources enter, wastes and heat leave, governance reads the environment and directs the work processes. What is missing is a product: "Notice what is not shown in the figure. There is no 'product' or 'service' output from the HSS returning something of value back to entities in the environment." Every subsystem of a supra-system owes it a function; open this model and count the outward flows that are not waste. There are none, and that is Mobus's finding, not a gap in the drawing.
